elements.sub: Summary of steps for every problem

items.meaning: Pick the simpler equation and write one variable in terms of the other (e.g. x in terms of y).
Substitute this value into the OTHER equation to get a single linear equation.
Put the obtained value into the rearranged equation to find the second variable.

elements.text: How can we verify our solution is 100% correct?
How do you verify whether a solution (x, y) is correct?
LHS = RHS in Equation 1 AND Equation 2 confirms the solution 100%.

beats.topic: The idea of replacing one thing with another
beats.narration: Imagine you walk into a stationery shop to buy a pen and a notebook.

beats.topic: The idea of replacing one thing with another
The idea of replacing one thing with another
beats.narration: Now, the shopkeeper tells you one extra detail: the notebook costs exactly 30 rupees more than the pen.

beats.topic: The idea of replacing one thing with another
beats.narration: How could you use that fact to find the cost of just the pen without guessing?

ask.question: If y is equal to x + 30, what can you do with the 'y' in the first equation?
ask.expect: Replace y in the first equation with x + 30 so there is only one variable left.
ask.hint: Look at the first equation x + y = 50. What if you wrote (x + 30) wherever you see y?

options.text: Replace y with x + 30 in the first equation
options.why: Exactly — since y and (x + 30) are identical in value, you swap one for the other.

options.text: Add the two equations directly together
options.why: Adding them is elimination, which also works, but substitution specifically replaces one variable using its equivalent expression.
options.hint: Try replacing the letter y with what y is equal to.

options.text: Guess values until they add up to 50
options.why: Guessing takes trial and error, while substitution gives you an exact equation with only one variable.
options.hint: Look at what y equals in the second equation and put that into the first.

beats.topic: Expressing one variable in terms of the other
beats.narration: Let us take a standard textbook pair of linear equations.

beats.topic: Expressing one variable in terms of the other
beats.narration: Look closely at both equations. We want to isolate one variable completely on one side.

beats.topic: Expressing one variable in terms of the other
beats.narration: In equation 2, x has a coefficient of 1, which makes it much easier to isolate without dealing with fractions right away.

beats.topic: Expressing one variable in terms of the other
beats.narration: Now, where must we substitute this expression for x?

ask.question: Should we substitute x = 3 - 2y back into Equation 2 or into Equation 1?
ask.expect: Equation 1, because putting it back into Equation 2 will just give 3 = 3.
ask.hint: If you got the expression from Equation 2, what happens if you plug it right back into the same equation?

options.why: Right! If you plug it back into the equation it came from, all variables cancel out into an identity like 3 = 3.

options.text: Into Equation 2 where it came from
options.why: If you substitute back into Equation 2, you get (3 - 2y) + 2y = 3, which just says 3 = 3 and tells us nothing new.
options.hint: Always substitute into the other equation that hasn't been used yet.

beats.narration: Let us substitute x = (3 - 2y) into Equation 1: 7x - 15y = 2.
Now expand the bracket carefully by multiplying 7 with both terms inside.
Combine the like terms: minus 14y and minus 15y give minus 29y.
We have found our first value! What is our final step to find x?

ask.question: How do we find the value of x now that we know y = 19/29?
ask.expect: Substitute y = 19/29 back into the expression x = 3 - 2y.
ask.hint: Remember Equation 3, where x was already written in terms of y?

options.why: Yes! Equation 3 is already solved for x, so it gives x with the least calculation.

options.text: Start the entire method over again isolating y first
options.why: You do not need to restart! You already know y, so just plug that number directly into any equation.
options.hint: Put the numerical value of y back into x = 3 - 2y.

beats.narration: Every substitution problem follows the exact same four systematic steps.
Before you finish your exam answer, how can you be completely certain your values for x and y are correct?

ask.question: How do you verify whether a solution (x, y) is correct?
ask.expect: Plug both values back into the original equations to check if LHS equals RHS in both.
ask.hint: If you put your numbers back into the very first two equations, what should happen?

options.text: Substitute x and y into both original equations to see if LHS equals RHS
options.why: Spot on. If LHS equals RHS in both original equations, your solution is guaranteed to be correct.

options.text: Check only the equation you solved first
options.why: Checking only one equation is risky because a wrong pair might satisfy one equation but fail the other.
options.hint: A solution to a system must satisfy BOTH equations simultaneously.
